maths_errors.text: Doubling the circumference angle to get the centre angle instead of halving the centre angle — getting 224° instead of 56°.
maths_errors.correction: Doubling the circumference angle (56°) gives 56° × 2 = 112°, which is the correct centre angle, not 224°. The answer 224° comes from doubling the centre angle (112° × 2 = 224°). The mistake should read: 'Doubling the centre angle instead of halving it — getting 224° instead of 56°.'

maths_errors.text: Two angles in the same segment (same side of a chord) are equal.
maths_errors.correction: Being on the same side of a chord is not enough. The angles must be subtended by that chord: their arms must go to the two ends of the chord. Correct version: 'Angles subtended by the same chord (or arc) at points on the circumference in the same segment are equal.'

false_mistakes.text: Doubling the circumference angle to get the centre angle instead of halving the centre angle
false_mistakes.why: As worded, the 'mistake' is a valid method. Doubling the circumference angle is exactly how you find the centre angle (centre = 2 × circumference). The error that actually produces 224° is doubling the centre angle.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: identify and apply circle definitions and properties, including: centre, radius, chord, diameter, circumference
missing_spec_content.why: Radius, diameter and chord are used but never defined. The only definition given is 'circumference is the distance all the way round' (slides[1].formulaExplained). There is no explanation of what a chord is, or that a diameter is a chord through the centre.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: including: tangent, arc, sector and segment
missing_spec_content.why: 'Sector' does not appear anywhere in the lesson. 'Arc' is used ('same arc', 'major arc') without a definition. 'Segment' is only hinted at ('same side of a chord'). 'Tangent' is used without a definition: the lesson does not say it is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point.

density.text: Circumference = πd  or  2πr  |  Area = πr²  |  Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc)  |  Angle in a semicircle = 90°  |  Angles in the same segment are equal  |  Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°  |  Tangent is perpendicular to radius at the point of contact
density.why: Seven separate rules in one line, mixing mensuration with five different theorems. A first-time learner cannot take this in at once.

density.text: For angle theorems: an angle at the centre is exactly double the angle at the circumference when both are subtended by the same arc. An angle inscribed in a semicircle is always 90°. Two angles in the same segment (same side of a chord) are equal. In a cyclic quadrilateral (all four vertices on the circle), opposite angles add to 180°. A tangent meets the radius at exactly 90°.
density.why: Five theorems in one paragraph with no diagram. 'Subtended', 'inscribed' and 'segment' are used without explanation.

density.text: A set of angle rules governs triangles and quadrilaterals drawn inside or on circles — these are circle theorems, and they all follow from the symmetry of the circle.
density.why: One sentence carries several ideas: what the rules apply to, their name, and why they are true. The claim 'follow from the symmetry' is never explained.

density.text: both are subtended by arc AB
density.why: 'Subtended' is a key term that is never defined anywhere in the lesson.

density.text: If they're on opposite sides, they are supplementary (add to 180°), not equal.
density.why: This introduces a new result with no reason given. It actually comes from the cyclic quadrilateral rule, and the lesson never makes that link.

density.text: Circumference = distance around the edge → 2πr or πd (one factor of r). Area = space inside → πr² (r squared).
density.why: Arrow chains and the bracketed idea 'one factor of r' are not explained.

density.text: Doubling the circumference angle to get the centre angle instead of halving the centre angle — getting 224° instead of 56°.
density.why: The wording contradicts the numbers given, so a student cannot work out what the error actually is.
